extracted.intended_audience: classical readers; students and scholars of Greek literature; poets, dramatists, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical guidance (from Aristotle's Poetics, trans. S. H. Butcher) for composing, structuring, and judging poetry—especially tragedy—including the means/objects/manner of imitation, elements of tragedy, plot rules, character, diction, and methods for answering criticisms. Emphasises plot primacy, unity, probability/necessity, and the proper generation of tragic emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the common principle
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Imitation’ the common principle of the Arts of Poetry, Music, Dancing, Painting, and Sculpture: artistic production is fundamentally imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle frames all poetic and allied arts as forms of mimesis; this provides the basis for distinguishing species of poetry by their means, objects, and manner of imitation. Use this notion to evaluate whether a work truly renders an imitation and how that shapes its aims and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of imitation: rhythm, language, and harmony (melody)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Means of Imitation are Rhythm, Language, and ‘Harmony’ (or Melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different arts and poetic genres employ these means in different combinations (e.g. dancing uses rhythm alone; flute/lyre use rhythm+melody; poetry uses language). When judging or composing, ensure the chosen means suit the genre and that their combination is appropriate and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation: higher or lower types
rubrics_metrics.description: The Objects of Imitation are persons acting, represented either as better than in real life, worse than in real life, or as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice underlies the distinction between Tragedy (portrays men better than in life) and Comedy (portrays men worse). Assess whether the moral/psychological type represented fits the genre and the intended ethical/aesthetic effect (examples: Homer portrays nobler men; Aristophanes worse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation: narrative vs dramatic (or mixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be in form either dramatic, narrative, pure narrative (including lyric), or pure drama; the poet may imitate by narration (speaking in another person or his own unchanged person) or by representing actors who live and move before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work should present actions by enacted characters or by narrated speech; this choice affects immediacy, unity, and emotional impact. Evaluate how the chosen manner serves the imitation of action and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy and its six elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is defined and said to have six elements: three external—Scenic Presentment (opsis), Lyrical Song (melopoeia), Diction (lexis); and three internal—Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), and Thought (dianoia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating tragic poetry, identify and judge each element; Plot is of primary importance, followed by Character and Thought. External elements (spectacle, song, diction) matter but are subordinate to the internal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot, or the representation of the action, is of primary importance; Character and Thought come next in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the plot constitutes the central organizing principle: does it present a coherent sequence of incidents that generates the intended moral/emotional effects? Weak plots undermine the whole work regardless of good diction or spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole: complete and of adequate magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Whole’ means a self-contained action with a beginning, middle, and end; 'adequate magnitude' means sufficient size to produce the intended catharsis without dilution or unnecessary extension. Evaluate economy and completeness of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Plot consists not in Unity of Hero, but in Unity of Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity requires that all incidents contribute organically to the single action; it's an organic connectedness of parts, not merely focusing on a single protagonist. Judge whether extraneous episodes or characters distract from the central action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic connection of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts must be organically connected; dramatic unity is attained by observing poetic (universal) rather than historical (particular) truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each episode/scene should follow necessarily or probably from what precedes; avoid episodic or loosely connected sequences. Prefer coherence grounded in causal and probable relations appropriate to the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of probable or necessary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule of probable or necessary sequence as applied to the incidents: poetic sequence follows probability or necessity rather than mere factual chronology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents so that they follow by cause/probability/necessity in the logic of the imitation; this preserves unity and plausibility. When assessing plot logic, test whether transitions are necessary/probable within the poetic world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best tragic effects combine the inevitable and the unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Tragic effects depend on the combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design reversals and recognitions so they feel both unforeseen and necessary in retrospect. Evaluate whether shocking events are structured to seem both surprising and plausibly arising from the plot's causal chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and use of Simple and Complicated plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple (haploi) plots are without reversal and recognition; Complicated (peplegmenoi) plots include elements like reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the plot type according to the desired emotional outcome. Complicated plots (with peripeteia and anagnorisis) are often more felicitous for producing pity and fear; evaluate whether such devices are earned and properly integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal), Anagnorisis (recognition), and Pathos (passion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden Reversal of Fortune (peripeteia), Recognition (anagnorisis), and Tragic or disastrous Incident (pathos) are defined and explained as technical elements of plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and judge the varieties of recognition and reversal; these are central devices for producing catharsis. Check examples for natural causal progression and psychological plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of Tragedy (quantitative parts): prologue, episode, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘quantitative parts’ (merê kata to poson) of Tragedy are defined—Prologue, Episode, etc.—(passage probably an interpolation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the named parts as a checklist for structural composition: ensure prologue sets up the action, episodes develop it, and other parts fulfill their roles in the overall unity. Be cautious when treating interpolated material as prescriptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic emotions (pity and fear) must spring from the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should spring out of the Plot itself. To produce them by the Scenery or Stage Spectacle is entirely against the spirit of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate emotional effect by examining if feelings are provoked by character and incident, not merely by external spectacle. Avoid reliance on scenic showmanship to manufacture pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as manifestation of moral purpose; rules of probability/necessity apply
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of Character (as the manifestation of moral purpose) in Tragedy: requisites of ethical portraiture; the rule of necessity or probability is applicable to Character as to Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge characters for coherent moral motivation and for actions that follow from their nature; avoid characters acting irrationally without necessity. Idealisation is allowed insofar as character remains probable within the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous irrationality or Deus ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘Deus ex Machina’ (a passage out of place here) is criticized; irrational or depraved elements are censured where there is no inner necessity for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolutions or incidents introduced without necessity weaken unity and plausibility. Evaluate whether improbable or irrational elements are justified by inner artistic reasons; remove or revise gratuitous contrivances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition: various kinds and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition (anagnorisis) occurs in various kinds—by tokens, by change of fortune, by the poet’s devices—with illustrative examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When employing recognition, pick a type that fits the plot mechanics (token, logical inference, revelation) and ensure it follows naturally from prior material; judge whether the recognition produces the intended cathartic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical composition rules for the tragic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules: (1) To place the scene before his eyes, and to act the parts himself to enter into vivid sympathy with the dramatis personae; (2) To sketch the bare outline of the action before proceeding to fill in the episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embodied imagination and preliminary plotting: enactivity and outlining help achieve vivid, coherent actions. Assess composition process for these practices to be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further compositional rules: complication, dénouement, balance, and chorus integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Further rules: (1) be careful about the Complication and Dénouement of the Plot, especially the Dénouement; (2) to unite, if possible, varied forms of poetic excellence; (3) not to overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry; (4) to make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay special attention to the resolution; avoid mixing epic excess into tragedy; integrate choral odes so they advance or reflect the action rather than interrupt it. Judge the harmony and fit of these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) and Diction (lexis): modes of expressing the intellectual element
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (dianoia), or the Intellectual element, and Diction in Tragedy: Thought may be expressed either by the dramatic speeches composed according to rules of rhetoric or through dramatic incidents which speak for themselves; Diction falls largely within the domain of the Art of Declamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how ideas are conveyed—by speech or by incident—and whether diction serves clarity, dramatic appropriateness, and rhetorical effectiveness. Consider also metrical and grammatical appropriateness where noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic diction: elevation combined with perspicuity; admissible words and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic Diction combines elevation of language with perspicuity; passages discuss admissible words and modes of speech, including Metaphor in particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess diction for elevated tone without obscurity; metaphors should be apt and enhance rather than cloud meaning. Judge poetic vocabulary choices by clarity and appropriateness to character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: agreements and critical differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic Poetry agrees with Tragedy in Unity of Action but differs in length, metre, and the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction; tragedy achieves concentrated effect within narrower limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing form, align scale and devices to the genre: epic allows breadth and episodic parts, tragedy demands unity, concision, and concentrated emotional arc. Evaluate whether the chosen form’s conventions are respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth (universal) vs historical truth (particular); standard for plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic (poetic) truth expresses the Universal; Plot and incidents should follow poetic truth rather than mere historical particularity. A 'probable impossibility' is preferable to an improbable possibility when it better serves the poetic end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge implausible events by whether they satisfy poetic plausibility and exemplify universal truths; require inner artistic justification for departures from ordinary plausibility. Apply the standard that the poetic exemplar may surpass reality if it better serves the end of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of critical objection and method of answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections are drawn from five sources—objects censured as impossible, irrational, morally hurtful, inconsistent, or inaccurate with regard to a special art; answers should be sought under twelve heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or critiquing a work, classify objections into these five types and formulate responses according to the systematic types Aristotle proposes (the 'twelve' heads referenced). This gives a diagnostic framework for critical debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude and concentrated pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of tragedy is achieved within narrower limits; a concentrated effect (brief, unified action) is more pleasurable than a long-drawn imitation diluted by length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an appropriate temporal and narrative magnitude to achieve the intended cathartic pleasure; avoid spreading the action so far that the emotional force is diluted. Evaluate whether the plot's scale serves concentration of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency: examine contradictions by standards of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistencies should be examined by whether the poet contradicts what he says himself or what a reasonable person would assume (dialectical refutation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test apparent contradictions against the internal logic of the poem and the reasonable assumptions of characters; criticisms should distinguish between genuine inconsistency and plausible interpretive readings.
